performers: Nancy O’Doan and Neal O’Doan, pianos
intro: A ballroom emerges from the bottom of two pianos, then the waltz spins itself to pieces. Nancy and Neal O’Doan play Ravel’s own two-piano version of La Valse.

sections.label: Intro · Low figures behind the curtain
sections.mNote: Bass notes turn beneath fragments of waltz melody

sections.label: A · The waltz takes the floor
sections.mNote: Longer tunes emerge over the three-beat accompaniment

sections.label: Dev · The waltzes return in fragments
sections.mNote: Earlier tunes break into shorter phrases

sections.label: Dev · Chords crowd the dance

cues.title: Below the ballroom
cues.text: The first piano starts with a quiet, low figure; the second adds a bass pulse. Bits of tune appear above them, then vanish. Ravel marks the opening Mouvement de Valse viennoise, though the ballroom is still hidden.
cues.evidence: Ravel’s two-piano transcription, Durand (1920), plate D. & F. 9897, p. 1. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/c/ce/IMSLP06112-Ravel_-_La_Valse_(trans._Ravel_-_2_pianos).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The dancers come into view
cues.text: The fragments lengthen into waltz phrases. One piano carries the tune while the other keeps little rising and falling figures moving beneath it. A bass note and its answering chords give the dance its three-beat step.
cues.evidence: Durand two-piano score, pp. 4–5, from letter A: melody in the first piano over second-piano figures.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Vienna on Ravel’s desk
cues.text: In 1906 Ravel plans a work called Wien, after Vienna, as a tribute to Johann Strauss. It waits until 1919–20 to become La Valse. The title changes; his love of the dance survives.
cues.evidence: Calvin Dotsey, Houston Symphony programme essay, documents the 1906 Wien project and later composition: https://houstonsymphony.org/ravel-la-valse/.

cues.title: Diaghilev says no
cues.text: In 1920 Ravel and Marcelle Meyer play the two-piano score for Diaghilev. Poulenc remembers the impresario’s verdict: “It’s the portrait of a ballet.” Ravel quietly gathers his manuscript and leaves the room.
cues.evidence: Francis Poulenc’s recollection of the 1920 audition, quoted by Calvin Dotsey: https://houstonsymphony.org/ravel-la-valse/. Harald Hodeige also recounts it: https://www.berliner-philharmoniker.de/en/programme-notes/maurice-ravel-la-valse/.

cues.title: The old tunes splinter
cues.text: The waltzes return in pieces. A phrase starts, breaks off, and meets another familiar figure; the bass keeps turning beneath them. The graceful tunes now have to compete for room.
cues.evidence: The second half’s return and recombination of earlier waltz themes are described by Calvin Dotsey: https://houstonsymphony.org/ravel-la-valse/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Chandeliers in eighteen fifty-five
cues.text: Ravel’s printed scene begins among whirling clouds. They part to reveal couples in an immense ballroom; the chandeliers blaze. He dates the scene precisely: “Une Cour impériale, vers 1855” — “An imperial court, around 1855”.
cues.evidence: Ravel’s scenario, printed before p. 1 of the Durand two-piano score (1920); our translation of the final sentence.

cues.title: The waltz loses a beat
cues.text: Ravel writes Pressez jusqu’à la fin: press on to the end. The two pianos hammer out repeated waltz figures, then a bar of two beats breaks the triple metre. The last bass note lands with an accent.
cues.evidence: Durand two-piano score, p. 42: Pressez jusqu’à la fin, final 2/4 bar and accented closing bass.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A tune rises above the bass
transitions.from: Intro · Low figures behind the curtain
transitions.to: A · The waltz takes the floor
transitions.how: The opening’s low repeated notes lead into letter A, where the second piano keeps a running figure beneath the first piano’s melody. Bass notes still mark the dance step. The tune grows into longer phrases, marked en dehors, above the quiet accompaniment.
transitions.evidence: Durand two-piano score (1920), pp. 4–5, letter A.

source.title: Ravel, La valse — composer’s two-piano transcription, Durand, 1920
source.locator: Ravel’s two-piano version, plate D. & F. 9897, pp. 1–42. Both players share the piano row.

timeline.note: Two pianos share the waltzes: one carries a melody while the other supplies bass notes, chords and rushing scales.

composer.epithet: He made a ballet from two tunes and a snare drum, and gave his war dead a suite of dances.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; Fauré for composition, André Gedalge for counterpoint
Ricardo Viñes · Maurice Delage · Tristan Klingsor · M. D. Calvocoressi

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: To M. D. Calvocoressi, recalled in his Musicians Gallery (1933)

composer.background:
Ravel’s father took his sons to factories to see the machinery. His mother sang to them. Pierre-Joseph was a Swiss-born engineer; Marie Delouart was Basque and had grown up in Madrid. Maurice was born in Ciboure on 7 March 1875, and the family moved to Paris three months later. He kept returning to the Basque coast, and Spain kept returning in his music: the plucked-guitar attacks of Alborada del gracioso, the habanera that rocks through the Rapsodie espagnole, the clocks ticking in a Toledo shop in L’heure espagnole.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire at fourteen, studied piano with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot and lost his place in 1895 for failing to win the required prizes. Two teachers then understood him: André Gedalge, who gave him counterpoint lessons from 1897, and Fauré, whose composition class he entered in January 1898. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, became the pianist his music needed. Viñes gave the first performances of Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit, pieces their composer could never have played with comparable command.
